story_text.value:
Hi HN, I'm sushi. I built ParkourNote, a personal knowledge management app that currently focuses on research: finding papers, reading PDFs, asking AI about them, and writing.

A few things it does:

Describe a topic, and an agent creates a project, searches arXiv, and imports relevant papers The PDF reader previews citations on hover, overlays translations on the page, and shows original and translated text side by side The agent sees the page you're reading and your selection; you can also connect Claude or ChatGPT via MCP A block editor with math support that compiles LaTeX / Typst to PDF

Demo (7 min): https://youtu.be/yZs2nQJtgkg

ParkourNote is just me. I built it in about a month: the web app, a Flutter mobile app, and a Chrome extension. It isn't even my full-time job. I work on it for an hour or two in the morning before work, plus evenings and weekends.

Two things surprised me along the way:

- The web app uses BlockNote for Notion-style editing, but I wanted Flutter for mobile. I asked Claude to implement a compatible editor in Flutter. It took about a day, and it works: documents round-trip between web and mobile. - In high school I worked as a video editor for MarginNote. Back then, a single 5-minute video took about a month, from scripting to recording, editing, and animation. For ParkourNote, I made launch videos for the Chinese, English, Japanese, and Korean markets in one weekend, plus a second Chinese version cut for portrait viewing. I didn't open a video editor once. It was all done with Claude Opus 5.5.

PG recently posted something along the lines of: in the AI era, you want to be either very close to the users or very close to the intelligence. That resonated with me, but honestly, building this left me a bit lost. I find it hard to think of a consumer software feature that current AI can't build. So if anyone can build anything, where is the moat? I'm genuinely unsure.

The other side of it is exciting, though. Running ParkourNote alone, I feel less like a solo developer and more like a CEO of a small company: I manage product, engineering, marketing, and operations, and somehow it's all manageable. A one-person company feels genuinely possible now, in a way it didn't a few years ago.

Signup is required since the AI features cost money to run; new accounts get 100 free credits after email verification.

Happy to answer questions about the product, the workflow, or the moat question. I'd genuinely like to hear how others are thinking about it.

title.value: Show HN: ParkourNote – A research workspace, built solo in a month with Claude

story_text.value:
In early 2020, tensorflow was the dominant deep learning framework. So, deepface was built to run on top of tensorflow. Thereafter, pytorch becomes the dominant framework for deep learning. We got many requests from community to support pytorch.

In the latest release (v0.0.101), DeepFace can now run on top of PyTorch alongside TensorFlow!

Users has been installing deepface as `pip install deepface` commmand and this was installing its tensorflow dependency. Now, users should install the library as `pip install deepface[tensorflow]` or `pip install deepface[pytorch]` commands to install its deep learning framework dependency. To avoid releasing breaking change, the default `pip install deepface` command will continue to install tensorflow for a while.

Be appreciate it if you share your comments, feedbacks and opinions.

story_text.value:
I've been building Fusor. It's a reactive web framework for Rust where the templates are plain HTML files, so there's no markup living inside Rust macros like view! or rsx!.

The state and logic live in ordinary Rust structs, and the whole app compiles to WASM. It also benefits from Rust type checkers, even for the HTML bindings.

The Fusor website is fully built using the framework. It's all experimental, so I expect breaking changes and lots of refactors.

Any feedback is welcome, and so are contributions! The project is pro AI, if you do decide to contribute.

story_text.value:
I'm an American who got married to a Mauritian this past May. We had our Hindu wedding in my wife's home country of Mauritius. My family and friends are not Hindu, and certainly had never been to the tiny island of Mauritius (it's off the coast of Madagascar in case you were wondering).

My wife and I arrived in Mauritius only two weeks before the start of the wedding to put the final preparations in place. I dreaded the prospect of answering a billion questions from my guests while trying to do this. I also dreaded them not having a way to find the answers.

So I made an AI app that acted as a guest concierge. At first I simply made a wedding db, seeded it with our info, connected an MCP server with tools to it, connected the agent to it, and gave all my guests an invite link to use it.

Scope creep took over and now I have an entire AI platform for planning weddings and being a guest concierge. The two sides are actually really complementary to each other: to make the ai answer correctly, you need a knowledge base. So the wedding planning aspect just kind of happened as a result.

There's so much more to this and I'm more than happy to discuss everything I've learned -- for example, the number one thing my guests did with the ai on the day of the ceremony was try to jailbreak it.

The demo I'm sharing here is an example wedding where you get to act as a guest and can interact with the ai concierge. I hope you find it interesting!

title.value: Show HN: An AI wedding concierge I built and ran at my own 300-person wedding

story_text.value:
It improves the usual workflow: take a screenshot, switch to a chat tab, upload it, switch back. - Built with Rust and Tauri v2, including a built-in native screenshot solution for maximum performance and stability. - Answers come from OpenAI models. Fast, the default, usually starts answering within 1–2 seconds; Best is slightly slower, but provides a much higher quality response. - Free is 3 captures a day, up to 10 a week, on Fast, and needs an email sign-in, since usage is metered per account. Plus is $10/month: 2,500 credits a month, the Best model (25 credits per answer, follow-ups included; Fast is 1), and up to 10 follow-ups per capture instead of 2. - Windows 10/11, and Linux on Wayland (GNOME 45+ or KDE Plasma 6). No macOS yet, and no X11.

What I'd most like to know: 1. Is this workflow actually quicker than what you do now? 2. Squint Plus is currently $10/month or $99/year: a) At what monthly price would Plus feel like a good deal? b) At what price would it start to feel expensive, though you'd still consider it? c) At what price would it be too expensive to consider at all? 3. Did anything break during install, sign-in, or a capture?

Thanks!

story_text.value:
i kept collecting rare internal company docs + out-of-print business books in random folders, so i put them all on one page.

top shelf has docs like intel's 1968 investor memo, apple's original marketing philosophy, bill gates' internet tidal wave memo, yahoo's peanut butter manifesto, facebook's little red book, valve's handbook, and mrbeast's onboarding doc.

bottom shelf has hard-to-find books from the founders/leaders of ibm, hp, gm, fastenal and others.

everything links to a free legal source. original pdf/scan when i could find one, otherwise internet archive.

if you know any rare docs or books that belong here, send them my way.
